logline: A West Yorkshire police sergeant haunted by her daughter's suicide confronts the man she holds responsible - a violent ex-con whose orbit keeps pulling back into her family's life across three series.

seasons.review_body: Series 1 aired on BBC One in spring 2014, earning 96 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 26 critics and an 83 on Metacritic. It won the BAFTA for Best Drama Series in 2015. Sarah Lancashire's Catherine Cawood - a police sergeant holding herself together through routine and dark humour while dealing with personal catastrophe - was immediately identified as one of the great characters in British television. Critics noted that Sally Wainwright's writing resisted procedural convention: the series is less interested in the mechanics of crime than in how violence radiates through a community and what it costs people who absorb it professionally. HitFix called it 'so effective at what it sets out to do, and so neat in fitting all its pieces together.' The Calderdale landscape became a character in itself.

bollymeter.basis: Metacritic 84; won BAFTA Best Drama Series 2017. Critics praised the series for expanding its world without softening the moral complexity that defined Series 1.

seasons.review_body: Series 2 aired in February 2016 to continued critical acclaim, earning an 84 on Metacritic and winning a second consecutive BAFTA for Best Drama Series. The series expanded the world of the first - introducing new crimes and new characters - while maintaining the same unsentimental moral framework. Critics noted that Wainwright's writing had become more ambitious: the central trauma was still present but the show was now juggling multiple parallel investigations without losing its character-centred focus. Lancashire's performance was again singled out as the engine of the series. The second BAFTA confirmed the show's position as the prestige standard for British crime drama.
seasons.season_over_season: Series 2 widened the canvas and deepened the supporting ensemble, winning a second BAFTA while maintaining the tonal precision and moral seriousness of Series 1.

bollymeter.basis: 100 percent on Rotten Tomatoes from 45 reviews; Metacritic 93. The Guardian called the finale 'brutal, tender, funny, compelling and heartbreaking.' Critics cited it as one of the finest endings in British television.

seasons.review_body: The final series aired from 1 January 2023, reaching a 100-percent Rotten Tomatoes score from 45 reviews and a Metacritic of 93. The seven-year gap since Series 2 gave the characters time to change in ways that felt earned rather than imposed: Ryan, the son Catherine raised after her daughter's suicide, was now a teenager with his own relationship to his father's incarceration. Critics unanimously called the series finale one of the most accomplished endings in British television. The Guardian's Lucy Mangan described it as 'brutal, tender, funny, compelling and heartbreaking.' The Atlantic praised Lancashire as a character who is 'fearless, moody, perceptive, abrasive, indispensable.' The season's 93 Metacritic score was the show's best.
seasons.season_over_season: The seven-year gap paid dividends: characters had aged and shifted in ways that made the resolution feel earned, and the final episode delivered on every emotional promise the series had accumulated.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 6
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale of Happy Valley closes out Catherine Cawood's story with the series' most emotionally concentrated writing. Critics who had called the show one of British television's finest were unanimous that the ending justified nine years of investment. The Guardian called it 'brutal, tender, funny, compelling and heartbreaking' in what reads as a genuine rave from a publication not given to superlatives.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The final confrontation between Catherine and Tommy Lee Royce, years in the making, in the last episode of the series.
